title: Late Period but Not Pregnant? 9 Common Reasons
description: Late period but not pregnant? Learn why your period might be late, what a negative pregnancy test means, how late a period can be and when to see a GP.
imageAlt: Mochi, a pink mascot, sitting beside a calendar with a thoughtful expression, a small thought cloud and an hourglass
intro: Your period can be late even when you're not pregnant, and common reasons include stress, weight changes, exercise and hormonal fluctuations. Sometimes, your cycle is simply a little longer than usual. Understanding what can delay your period, when to take a pregnancy test and when to speak to a GP can help you decide what to do next.

how-late.title: How late can a period be before it counts as late?

paragraphs.first: Your period is considered late when it hasn't arrived by the date you normally expect it. According to the NHS, the average menstrual cycle is about 28 days, but it can naturally be shorter or longer. A gap of 21 to 35 days between the start of your periods is generally considered regular.
paragraphs.second: To work out whether your period is late, start counting from the first day of your last period. Your cycle length is the number of days from that day to the first day of your next period. If your cycles usually last 28 days and you're now on day 32 without bleeding, your period is three days late.
paragraphs.third: A late period can also mean that you ovulated later than usual. According to Cleveland Clinic, the luteal phase, which is the time between ovulation and your next period, lasts about 14 days on average. If stress or illness delays ovulation, your period may arrive later too, even if you're not pregnant.

pregnancy-first.title: What does a late period with a negative pregnancy test mean?

paragraphs.first: A late period with a negative pregnancy test may mean you're not pregnant, but it can also mean you've tested too early. If there is any possibility of pregnancy, taking a test is the first step before considering other reasons for your delayed period.
paragraphs.second: According to the NHS, most home pregnancy tests are most reliable from the first day of a missed period. If your cycles are irregular or you don't know when your next period is due, take a test at least 21 days after your last unprotected sex. You can use a urine sample taken at any time of day.
paragraphs.third: The NHS explains that a positive pregnancy test result is almost certainly correct, while a negative result is less reliable. Testing too early or not following the instructions correctly can lead to a negative result even if you're pregnant. Hormonal contraception, including the pill, does not stop a pregnancy test from working.

pregnancy-first.note: If your pregnancy test is negative and your period still hasn't arrived, wait a few days and test again. If your second test is also negative and you still haven't had your period, the NHS recommends speaking to a GP.

common-reasons.title: Why is my period late if I'm not pregnant?

paragraphs.first: If you're not pregnant, common reasons for a late period include stress, weight changes, excessive exercise, hormonal contraception and certain medical conditions. Your cycle can also vary naturally from one month to the next, without there being an underlying health problem.
paragraphs.second: According to the NHS, late and missed periods can happen for a range of reasons, from everyday lifestyle changes to hormonal conditions. Thinking about recent changes in your health, routine or contraception may help you understand why your period hasn't arrived, although symptoms alone cannot confirm the cause.

items.stress: Physical or emotional stress can delay ovulation, causing your period to arrive later than expected.
items.weight-change: Sudden weight loss or being overweight can affect the hormones involved in regulating your menstrual cycle.
items.exercise: Exercising too much can disrupt your menstrual cycle and lead to late or missed periods.
items.contraception: Hormonal contraception, such as the combined pill, contraceptive injection or hormonal coil (IUS), can change or stop your periods.
items.breastfeeding: Breastfeeding can delay the return of your periods or make your menstrual cycle irregular.
items.pmos: Polycystic ovary syndrome, now referred to by the NHS as PMOS (formerly PCOS), can cause irregular, delayed or missed periods.
items.thyroid: An overactive or underactive thyroid can affect your menstrual cycle and cause late or missed periods.
items.perimenopause: Periods can become irregular during perimenopause, which usually begins between the ages of 45 and 55.
items.normal-variation: The gap between your periods can naturally vary, meaning your period may occasionally arrive later than usual.

stress-and-lifestyle.title: Can stress, weight changes or exercise delay your period?

paragraphs.first: Yes, stress, sudden weight loss, being overweight and doing too much exercise can all cause a late or missed period without pregnancy. These factors can affect the hormones that regulate your menstrual cycle, sometimes delaying ovulation and, as a result, the arrival of your next period.
paragraphs.second: According to Cleveland Clinic, the luteal phase, which begins after ovulation, lasts about 14 days on average. When you ovulate later than usual, your period generally arrives later too. This helps explain why your cycle might suddenly become longer during a particularly stressful month.
paragraphs.third: For example, imagine you're going through a stressful exam season and ovulate a week later than usual. Your period may also arrive around a week later than expected. Even if your exams are over by the time your period is due, the earlier delay in ovulation can still affect its timing.
paragraphs.fourth: The NHS also identifies sudden weight loss, being overweight and excessive exercise as possible causes of missed or late periods. If you've recently changed your eating habits or exercise routine, these changes may help explain a longer cycle. Speak to a GP if your usual menstrual pattern changes or your periods become irregular.

contraception-and-breastfeeding.title: Can contraception or breastfeeding make your period late?

paragraphs.first: Yes, hormonal contraception and breastfeeding can both cause late, irregular or missed periods. According to the NHS, contraceptive methods such as the combined pill, contraceptive injection and hormonal intrauterine system (IUS), also known as the hormonal coil, can affect when or whether you bleed.
paragraphs.second: Missing a period or having no bleeding at all can be expected with some hormonal contraceptive methods. Check the patient information leaflet for your particular method or ask a pharmacist if you're unsure what to expect. If you think you could be pregnant, remember that hormonal contraception does not stop a pregnancy test from working.
paragraphs.third: Breastfeeding can also delay the return of your periods after giving birth, and your cycles may be irregular when they return. If you're breastfeeding and unsure whether a missed period could be related to pregnancy, taking a pregnancy test can help you work out what to do next.

health-conditions.title: What health conditions can cause a late or missed period?

paragraphs.first: Several health conditions can cause late or missed periods even when you're not pregnant. The NHS lists polycystic ovary syndrome, now referred to as PMOS (formerly PCOS), an overactive or underactive thyroid, diabetes and heart disease among the possible causes. A late period alone does not mean you have any of these conditions.
paragraphs.second: Perimenopause is another possible explanation, particularly if you're between the ages of 45 and 55. This is the transition towards menopause, during which your periods may become irregular. You might notice that the gap between your periods changes, even if your cycles have been predictable for many years.
paragraphs.third: According to the NHS, you should speak to a GP if you've missed a period and also notice weight gain or loss, tiredness, facial hair growth, or unusually dry or oily skin. These symptoms can have several explanations, so they cannot tell you on their own why your period is late.

when-to-see-a-gp.title: When should you see a doctor about a late period?

paragraphs.first: You should see a GP if you've missed three periods in a row, your periods have become irregular or you've noticed other symptoms alongside a missed period. You don't need to wait until you've missed three periods if your usual menstrual pattern has changed or you're experiencing other symptoms.
paragraphs.second: The NHS recommends seeking medical advice in the situations listed below. Keeping a record of your period dates, symptoms and pregnancy test results can help your GP understand what has changed and decide whether further checks are needed.

items.three-missed-periods: You've missed three periods in a row.
items.no-first-period: Your periods haven't started by the age of 15.
items.other-symptoms: You've missed a period and also notice weight gain or loss, tiredness, facial hair growth, or dry or oily skin.
items.irregular-pattern: Your periods have become irregular or your usual menstrual pattern has changed.
items.negative-pregnancy-tests: You've taken two pregnancy tests, both were negative, and your period still hasn't arrived.
items.bleeding-between-periods: You're experiencing bleeding between your periods.
items.trying-to-conceive: Your periods are irregular and you're struggling to get pregnant.

when-to-see-a-gp.note: Get urgent medical help if you have severe pain in your lower tummy or heavy vaginal bleeding, especially if you've had a positive pregnancy test. Seek urgent help for these symptoms even if you haven't taken a pregnancy test or your result was negative.

track-your-cycle.title: How can tracking your cycle help you notice a late period?

paragraphs.first: Tracking your menstrual cycle helps you understand what's normal for you and recognise when your period is later than usual. Rather than comparing your cycle with the average of 28 days, you can look at your own history and notice changes in the timing or regularity of your periods.
paragraphs.second: Mochi is a free and private period tracker for iPhone that lets you log your period dates, symptoms and moods without creating an account. It uses your own cycle history to estimate when your next period might arrive. These predictions are estimates, and Mochi cannot diagnose a health condition or confirm whether you're pregnant.
paragraphs.third: If your periods become irregular or you're concerned about a missed period, consider sharing your cycle log with your GP. Having your dates and symptoms recorded in one place can make it easier to describe what's changed, particularly when you're trying to remember details from several months ago.

how-late-normal.question: How late can a period be and still be normal?
how-late-normal.answer: A period can arrive a few days later than usual because menstrual cycles naturally vary. According to the NHS, a gap of 21 to 35 days between periods is generally considered regular. If your usual pattern changes or your periods become irregular, speak to a GP.

negative-test.question: Why is my period late but my pregnancy test is negative?
negative-test.answer: Your period may be late because of stress, delayed ovulation, weight changes, hormonal contraception or another cause unrelated to pregnancy. However, a negative pregnancy test can also mean you've tested too early. Wait a few days and test again, and speak to a GP if the second test is negative and your period still hasn't arrived.

stress-delay.question: Can stress delay your period?
stress-delay.answer: Yes, stress can delay ovulation and cause your period to arrive later than expected. According to Cleveland Clinic, the phase after ovulation lasts about 14 days on average, so ovulating a week later than usual could delay your period by around a week.

how-many-days.question: How many days late can a period be if you're not pregnant?
how-many-days.answer: There is no fixed number of days a period can be late when you're not pregnant, as it depends on your usual cycle and the reason for the delay. The NHS considers gaps of more than 35 days between periods irregular. Speak to a GP if your usual menstrual pattern changes or you've missed three periods in a row.

skip-a-month.question: Is it normal to skip a period if you're not pregnant?
skip-a-month.answer: Occasionally skipping a period can happen without pregnancy, particularly during times of stress, weight changes, breastfeeding or hormonal contraception use. If pregnancy is possible, take a pregnancy test to rule it out. Speak to a GP if you've missed three periods in a row, your usual pattern changes or you develop other symptoms.

see-doctor.question: When should I worry about a late period?
see-doctor.answer: You should speak to a GP if you've missed three consecutive periods, your periods have become irregular or you have symptoms such as weight changes, tiredness, facial hair growth, or dry or oily skin. You should also seek medical advice if you've taken two pregnancy tests that were negative and your period still hasn't arrived.
